newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl wants punctual EMU, no devaluations.
newsitem.headline: Kohl wants punctual EMU, no devaluations.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said on Wednesday that European monetary union should go ahead as planned in 1999 with as many countries as possible taking part that can fulfil strict entry terms on a sustained basis.
Addressing parliament, Kohl said any devaluations within the exchange rate grid of the European Monetary System (EMS) would be incompatible with the goal of a strong euro currency.
"We need the Euro -- not at any time. We don't want to delay it. We want it now," Kohl told deputies on the second day of Germany's final 1997 budget debate.
In an apparent reference to mounting calls in France for a devaluation of the franc, Kohl said such a move would damage prospects for keeping the euro hard.
"Suggestions to weaken the stability criteria or to devalue a certain currency in the European Monetary System are not compatible with this cause and are actually harmful for the future," Kohl said.

Kohl came under attack from Oskar Lafontaine, leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), for trying to enforce a currency stability pact on other countries which would further force up unemployment in close allies like France.
"With 18 million out of work in Europe, we don't need a stability pact, but a pact for jobs," Lafontaine said.
"We must rethink and not hold to a policy which is creating ever higher unemployment. I am concerned for Franco-German relations," he added.
Kohl reemphasised Germany's position that as many countries as possible should join monetary union, as long as they can meet the strict criteria set by the Maastricht treaty.
"We want a hard currency and don't want to get into a weak currency situation. That is not arrogance, but comes from our experience in Germany over the past 50 years," Kohl said.
